newsitem.title: GERMANY: German opposition SPD links tax talks to coal deal.
newsitem.headline: German opposition SPD links tax talks to coal deal.

text.p: Germany's Social Democrats (SPD) on Monday linked their willingness to rejoin talks with the government on tax reforms to the outcome of a meeting between Chancellor Helmut Kohl and miners' leaders over coal subsidies.
Oskar Lafontaine, leader of the opposition SPD, also said that restarting the talks on big tax cuts would only make sense if the Kohl government came up with new ideas.

"If there are no new proposals, there won't be any new talks between the SPD and coalition," Lafontaine said after a meeting of SPD leaders in Berlin. But he added: "Any measures that can fight unemployment will win our support."

Lafontaine abruptly pulled out of tax talks at the weekend in support of miners protesting against government plans to cut aid to Germany's loss-making coal mines from nine billion marks ($5.3 billion) this year to 3.8 billion in 2005.

Germany's 18 pits have been at a standstill since Friday, and 3,000 miners marched on Bonn on Monday to picket the headquarters of the parties in Kohl's coalition. Thousands more demonstrated across the Ruhr and Saar coalfields.

SPD chief whip Peter Struck said the alternative proposed by the IG Bergbau miners union to wind down yearly subsidies to 6.5 billion marks in 2005 was "the last offer". "The government would be well-advised to take back its decision," he added.

Miners' leaders are scheduled to meet Kohl on Tuesday. IG Bergbau leader Hans Berger called on Monday for a national coal conference. He added that the government's subsidy plans would push the unemployment rate up to 30 percent in mining regions.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel said a cross-party compromise on taxes was still possible by Easter if the talks resumed.

But he repeated a weekend threat to initiate legislation this Friday which would cut 30 billion marks in tax if the SPD did not return to the tax talks. "The country cannot let itself to fall prey to the whims of the SPD," he said in Munich.

Record post-war unemployment had driven both sides to the negotiating table to try to strike a deal which would avoid bitter and lengthy wrangling in parliament, where the SPD can veto tax measures through its upper house majority.
Politicians from both sides had been cosying up to each other, leading some commentators to speculate Germany could soon see its first grand coalition since the 1960s.

But that mood has been shattered, leaving left and right accusing each other of holding up reforms just as Germany tries to put 4.7 million unemployed back to work and get its finances into shape for European monetary union (EMU).

Peter Hintze, general secretary of Kohl's Christian Democrats, condemned "irresponsible agitation" by the SPD premiers of Germany's two coal states; North Rhine-Westphalia's (NRW) Johannes Rau and Lafontaine, who heads Saarland state.

Waigel said there was no linkage between taxes and coal. But Lafontaine said the government was calling on the NRW government to stump up an extra 700 million marks in coal aid, while the region would lose five billion marks in revenues under the coalition tax reforms.
To get the tax talks back on track, Lafontaine wants the government to agree to lighten the tax load on working families next year, and cut Germany's job-killing labour overheads.

German newspapers criticised the SPD for seizing on the coal clash as the first chance to let the tax talks fail, even though Waigel has said he was ready to yield to some SPD demands like protecting tax relief for shift work.
"If everything is as is seems, the coalition's plans to cut coal subsidies came at just the right time for SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine," the Handelsblatt financial daily commented.

Handelsblatt added that Lafontaine had gone into the talks with serious misgivings: "He is driven by the fear that the SPD is just doing the coalition's own work and will lose out again at the general elections in 1998 as a result." ($ = 1.707 German Marks)
